title: Property tax rates, private tree bylaw and audit plan
subtitle: Tax relief programs, four tree bylaw options for public input, value-for-money audits and a closed cybersecurity briefing.
overview: The committee recommended that Council approve the 2024 property tax ratios and tax rates {{vote:m2}}. This is the second step after the budget and also continues the low-income seniors and disabled tax relief program and the charitable rebate program. These set how the tax burden is shared across property types.

On the private tree protection by-law, the committee received the key issues and options report and directed staff to proceed with its recommendations {{vote:m3}}. No option was chosen. Four scope options will go to a second round of public engagement starting April 30, with an updated by-law targeted to return to Council in March 2025.

The committee also recommended approving the 2024-2026 Internal Audit Work Plan and the Value-for-Money Audit Review Framework, and received the updated Internal Audit Charter {{vote:m4}}. Two value-for-money reviews are planned for 2024. Earlier, Council met in closed session on a corporate cybersecurity assessment, and the Mayor reported that staff were given direction.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended that Council approve the 2024 property tax ratios and corresponding tax rates set out in the staff report.
The committee received the key issues and options report and directed staff to proceed with its recommendations, including taking four scope options to a second phase of public engagement.
The committee recommended approval of the 2024-2026 audit work plan.
The committee recommended approval of the framework that will guide two value-for-money reviews in 2024, and received the updated Internal Audit Charter.

debate: On property tax, one councillor asked why the report uses the median rather than the average assessed value for a single-family home. Staff said the median is what the assessment agency reports and has been used historically, and it is not skewed by very high-value properties.

A delegate urged that the tree by-law include transparent, effective enforcement, citing concern that past penalties were small and that notices have been ignored. The delegate favoured the option covering all private lots with trees of 20 cm or more.

Councillors asked how the by-law would affect infill housing and ordinary homeowners. Staff said they would look at equity, scaling permit fees and compensation, and a fee-for-service model, and the Mayor asked staff to consider a user-fee approach that avoids tax-base impact.

One councillor asked that the financial analysis include the benefits of keeping trees, such as stormwater and infrastructure savings, not just costs. Staff agreed. Councillors also raised root damage, invasive species such as buckthorn, and how residents would learn about the by-law, and staff said outreach would be added.

On the audit plan, councillors asked about outsourcing if resources fall short, how independence is kept, and why development approvals are not on the list. Staff said outsourcing funds exist and that the planning review is already under way. A proposal on back-office savings from a past service review was referred to corporate services.
